title: Mock 2 · Retirement Ready
blurb: Retirement maths and product limits plus core tax, estate and behaviour facts, with a short retirement-corpus caselet.

questions.q: What will Ravi's current monthly expense of ₹30,000 grow to by the time he retires?
questions.explanation: There are 25 years to retirement (60 − 35). FV = 30,000 × (1.06)^25 = ₹1,28,756 per month.
hints: Incorrect. This uses simple growth (30,000 × (1 + 0.06 × 25)), not compounding.
Incorrect. This compounds for only 24 years.
Incorrect. This compounds at the 8% investment return instead of 6% inflation.
questions.case: Ravi, aged 35, currently spends ₹30,000 per month on household expenses. He plans to retire at 60 and wants to maintain the same lifestyle, adjusted for inflation, which he expects to average 6% p.a. His retirement corpus is expected to earn 8% p.a. To estimate his retirement income need, his adviser starts from Ravi's detailed monthly budget, removes expenses that will stop (home-loan EMI, children's school fees) and adds heads that will rise (medical, travel). Ignore taxes.

questions.q: What inflation-adjusted (real) rate of return should be used to compute Ravi's retirement corpus?
questions.explanation: Real rate = (1 + 8%)/(1 + 6%) − 1 = 1.0189 − 1 = 1.89%, as used throughout the workbook.
hints: Incorrect. Simple subtraction (8% − 6%) is only an approximation.
Incorrect. This multiplies (1.08 × 1.06) instead of dividing.
Incorrect. This divides the wrong way round (1.06/1.08 − 1).
questions.case: Ravi, aged 35, currently spends ₹30,000 per month on household expenses. He plans to retire at 60 and wants to maintain the same lifestyle, adjusted for inflation, which he expects to average 6% p.a. His retirement corpus is expected to earn 8% p.a. To estimate his retirement income need, his adviser starts from Ravi's detailed monthly budget, removes expenses that will stop (home-loan EMI, children's school fees) and adds heads that will rise (medical, travel). Ignore taxes.

questions.q: Which method of estimating retirement income is the adviser using?
options: Replacement ratio method
Human Life Value method
Expense protection method
Needs-based insurance method
questions.explanation: The expense protection method defines retirement income from a detailed budget of expected expenses in retirement, adjusting heads that rise or fall. The replacement ratio method takes a % of pre-retirement income.
hints: Incorrect. The replacement ratio method uses a % of pre-retirement income, not the budget.
Incorrect. HLV estimates life insurance needs.
Correct. Starting from the budget and adjusting expense heads is the expense protection method.
Incorrect. The needs-based method estimates life cover, not retirement income.
questions.case: Ravi, aged 35, currently spends ₹30,000 per month on household expenses. He plans to retire at 60 and wants to maintain the same lifestyle, adjusted for inflation, which he expects to average 6% p.a. His retirement corpus is expected to earn 8% p.a. To estimate his retirement income need, his adviser starts from Ravi's detailed monthly budget, removes expenses that will stop (home-loan EMI, children's school fees) and adds heads that will rise (medical, travel). Ignore taxes.

questions.q: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938, after what period can a life insurance policy no longer be called in question on any ground?
options: 3 years from the date of the policy, risk commencement or revival, whichever is later
2 years from the date of issue
5 years from the date of the first premium
7 years from the date of revival only
questions.explanation: Section 45 (the incontestability clause) bars questioning a life policy after 3 years from the policy date, risk commencement or revival date, whichever is later. Within 3 years it may be repudiated for fraud.
hints: Correct. The incontestability period is 3 years.
Incorrect. 2 years is when a traditional policy acquires surrender value, not the incontestability period.
Incorrect. 5 years is the health insurance moratorium.
Incorrect. 7 years has no relevance here.

questions.q: Surinder holds a 20-year endowment policy with a sum assured of ₹12 lakh and premiums payable quarterly. He stops paying after 6 years. What is the paid-up sum assured?
questions.explanation: Paid-up SA = SA × premiums paid ÷ premiums payable. Quarterly over 20 years = 80 premiums. 6 years paid = 24 premiums. ₹12,00,000 × 24/80 = ₹3,60,000.
hints: Correct. ₹12 lakh × 24/80 = ₹3.6 lakh.
Incorrect. This would correspond to 5 years (20 premiums) paid.
Incorrect. ₹4 lakh would mean one-third of premiums paid.
Incorrect. This wrongly uses 12 of 20 premiums.

questions.q: A traditional non-linked life policy with full premiums paid is surrendered in the 3rd policy year. Its minimum guaranteed surrender value is what percentage of premiums paid?
questions.explanation: The minimum GSV is 30% of premiums paid in the 2nd year, 35% in the 3rd, 50% in years 4–7, rising to at least 90% in the last two policy years.
hints: Incorrect. 30% applies in the 2nd policy year.
Correct. Year 3 gives 35%.
Incorrect. 50% applies in years 4 to 7.
Incorrect. 90% applies in the last two policy years.

questions.q: Which statement about the no-claim bonus (NCB) in car insurance is correct?
options: It is attached to the car and passes to the buyer when the car is sold
It belongs to the insured and can be transferred to a new car he buys
It is capped at 25% of the own-damage premium
It is lost when the insured switches insurer at renewal
questions.explanation: NCB can go up to 50% of the own-damage premium after 5 claim-free years. It belongs to the insured person, not the car, and a new insurer gives it when the policy is shifted at renewal.
hints: Incorrect. The buyer of the old car is not eligible for the seller's NCB.
Correct. The NCB follows the owner, not the vehicle.
Incorrect. The maximum is 50% after 5 claim-free years.
Incorrect. The new insurer provides the NCB on shifting at renewal.

questions.q: Mrs. Rao's income just before retirement is ₹2,00,000 per month and her planner uses an 80% replacement ratio. What is her required income in the first month of retirement?
questions.explanation: Replacement income (Year 1) = pre-retirement income × 0.80 = ₹2,00,000 × 0.80 = ₹1,60,000. It is then increased by inflation each year.
hints: Incorrect. This assumes a 100% replacement ratio.
Incorrect. This is the 20% shortfall, not the replacement income.
Correct. 80% of ₹2 lakh = ₹1.6 lakh.
Incorrect. This uses a 60% ratio.

questions.q: Mohan's last drawn monthly wages were ₹52,000 and he completed 18 years and 8 months of continuous service. What gratuity is payable under the Code on Social Security, 2020 formula?
questions.explanation: Gratuity = 15 × last wages × years ÷ 26. Service of 18 years 8 months rounds up to 19 years because the extra part exceeds 6 months. 15 × 52,000 × 19 ÷ 26 = ₹5,70,000.
hints: Incorrect. This ignores rounding (uses 18 years).
Incorrect. This divides by 30 instead of 26.
Incorrect. This uses 30 days' wages instead of 15.
Correct. Round 8 months up: 15 × 52,000 × 19 ÷ 26 = ₹5.7 lakh.

questions.q: An NPS Tier I subscriber who has been investing for at least 3 years wants a partial withdrawal for a child's higher studies. How much can be withdrawn?
options: Up to 50% of the total corpus
Up to 25% of the subscriber's own contributions
Up to 25% of the total corpus including employer contributions and returns
The entire Tier I balance
questions.explanation: After 3 years a subscriber may withdraw up to 25% of their own contributions for specified purposes, up to 4 times before 60, with a minimum gap of 4 years between withdrawals.
hints: Incorrect. No 50% partial withdrawal rule exists.
Correct. The limit is 25% of own contributions.
Incorrect. The 25% applies to own contributions, not the full corpus.
Incorrect. Full withdrawal is allowed only at exit, subject to the annuity rules.

questions.q: Which statement about the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme (SCSS) is correct?
options: It has a 5-year term extendable in blocks of 3 years, with a maximum of ₹30 lakh across all accounts
Interest is paid monthly and is tax-free
Any resident aged 50 or above can open it
The maximum investment is ₹15 lakh per individual
questions.explanation: SCSS is for those aged 60 or above. The term is 5 years, extendable in blocks of 3 years, and the maximum across all accounts is ₹30 lakh. Interest is paid quarterly and is fully taxable.
hints: Correct. The 5 years, the 3-year extensions and the ₹30 lakh cap are all correct.
Incorrect. Interest is paid quarterly and is fully taxable.
Incorrect. The general age requirement is 60 years.
Incorrect. The limit is ₹30 lakh.

questions.q: A resident individual opting for the new tax regime under section 202 has a total income of exactly ₹12,00,000 (no special-rate income). What is his tax liability after the rebate?
options: Nil, because the rebate of up to ₹60,000 covers it
questions.explanation: Under the new regime, a resident with total income up to ₹12 lakh gets a rebate of up to ₹60,000 under s.156 (old s.87A). The tax on ₹12 lakh (₹20,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹60,000) is fully rebated.
hints: Correct. Tax of ₹60,000 is fully offset by the rebate.
Incorrect. This is the tax before the rebate.
Incorrect. ₹12,500 is the old-regime rebate limit.
Incorrect. This miscomputes the slab tax.

questions.q: Unlisted equity shares are treated as long-term capital assets when held for:
options: More than 12 months
More than 36 months
More than 24 months
More than 60 months
questions.explanation: Listed equity shares need more than 12 months, while unlisted shares need more than 24 months immediately before the transfer.
hints: Incorrect. 12 months applies to listed equity shares.
Incorrect. 36 months was an old rule and is no longer applicable.
Correct. Unlisted shares need more than 24 months.
Incorrect. No 60-month rule exists.

questions.q: Neeta, a resident, has a long-term capital gain of ₹3,00,000 on listed equity shares sold on a stock exchange with STT paid on both legs. She has no other capital gains. What is her tax (before surcharge and cess)?
hints: Incorrect. This ignores the ₹1.25 lakh exemption.
Incorrect. This applies 20% (the STCG rate) to the excess.
Incorrect. This applies 20% to the whole gain.

questions.q: For computing the salary perquisite on ESOPs, the fair market value of the shares is taken on which date?
options: The date of grant
The date of vesting
The date of sale of the shares
The date on which the employee exercises the option
questions.explanation: Perquisite = (FMV on the date of exercise − amount paid) × shares, taxed in the year of allotment. The FMV on the vesting or allotment date is not considered.
hints: Incorrect. Nothing is taxed at grant.
Incorrect. The workbook states the FMV on vesting is not considered.
Incorrect. The sale triggers capital gains, not the perquisite.
Correct. The FMV is taken on the exercise date.

questions.q: Ignoring grandfathering, what is the cost of acquisition of bonus shares allotted after 1 April 2001 without any payment?
options: Face value of the shares
Market price on the allotment date
Nil
Average cost of the original shares
questions.explanation: Bonus shares allotted without payment have a nil cost of acquisition (FMV on 1-4-2001 applies only to bonus shares issued before that date). The holding period runs from the allotment date.
hints: Incorrect. Face value is not used as cost.
Incorrect. The market price on allotment is not the cost.
Correct. The cost is nil.
Incorrect. The original shares' cost is not spread over the bonus shares (unlike a split).

questions.q: Under Muslim personal law, a widow whose deceased husband left children is entitled to what share of his property?
options: One-fourth
One-eighth
One-half
Two-thirds
questions.explanation: A Muslim widow takes 1/4 if there are no lineal descendants and 1/8 if there are children or grandchildren.
hints: Incorrect. 1/4 applies to a childless widow.
Correct. 1/8 when there are children.
Incorrect. 1/2 is the husband's share when there are no descendants (or a sole daughter's share).
Incorrect. 2/3 is the share of two or more daughters jointly.

questions.q: Under the Indian Succession Act, 1925, probate can be granted only to:
options: Any legal heir of the deceased
The eldest son of the deceased
The registrar who registered the Will
The executor appointed by the Will
questions.explanation: Section 222 states that probate is granted only to an executor appointed by the Will. Otherwise, letters of administration are issued.
hints: Incorrect. Legal heirs may get letters of administration, not probate.
Incorrect. Being the eldest son gives no right to probate.
Incorrect. The registrar has no role in granting probate.
Correct. Probate goes only to the executor.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT amount to revocation of a Will?
options: Executing a later Will that revokes it
The testator tearing the Will with the intention of revoking it
A written declaration of revocation executed like a Will
The Will being accidentally lost
questions.explanation: The workbook says the mere loss of a Will does not lead to revocation. A later Will or codicil, a written declaration executed like a Will, or destruction with intent all revoke it.
hints: Incorrect. A later duly executed Will is a mode of revocation.
Incorrect. Destruction with intent revokes the Will.
Incorrect. A declaration executed like a Will revokes it.
Correct. Loss without intent does not revoke a Will.

questions.q: An investor sells his winning stocks quickly but holds on to losing stocks hoping they will recover. This behaviour is known as the:
options: Anchoring effect
Home bias
Disposition effect
Framing effect
questions.explanation: Shefrin and Statman (1985) proposed the disposition effect, holding losers too long and selling winners too early, which flows from loss aversion.
hints: Incorrect. Anchoring is relying on pre-existing information.
Incorrect. Home bias is preferring domestic securities.
Correct. Selling winners and holding losers is the disposition effect.
Incorrect. Framing is answering differently depending on how a question is presented.

questions.q: According to the workbook, what is the FIRST step an adviser should take with a client who goes on shopping binges to relieve stress (retail therapy)?
options: Ask the client to stop using all bank accounts
Make the client conscious that the behaviour is induced by stress
Recommend a credit card with a high limit
Ignore it, since it reduces stress
questions.explanation: Step one is awareness that stress drives the behaviour. Step two is a specific budget, possibly in a separate account, as a self-imposed brake. Credit cards induce impulsive spending.
hints: Incorrect. This is not practical and is not the suggested approach.
Correct. Awareness comes first.
Incorrect. Credit cards encourage impulsive spending.
Incorrect. The adviser should help make such behaviour self-limiting.

questions.q: The investor's objective financial ability to absorb a loss without jeopardising goals, depending on income, assets, liabilities and time available, is called:
options: Risk tolerance
Risk composure
Risk perception
Risk capacity
questions.explanation: Risk capacity is the financial and temporal ability to absorb losses. A 35-year-old 30 years from retirement has more capacity than a 60-year-old near retirement, even with the same tolerance.
hints: Incorrect. Risk tolerance is willingness to accept uncertainty.
Incorrect. Risk composure is consistency of behaviour under stress.
Incorrect. Risk perception is how risky the investor judges something to be.
Correct. Ability (not willingness) is risk capacity.

questions.q: Other factors remaining the same, how does an increase in the number of dependants affect a person's risk appetite?
options: Risk appetite decreases
Risk appetite increases
Risk appetite is unaffected
Risk appetite first rises, then falls
questions.explanation: Table 18.1 shows risk appetite decreases as the number of dependent members increases, and increases as the number of earning members increases.
hints: Correct. More dependants means less appetite for risk.
Incorrect. Risk appetite increases with more earning members, not dependants.
Incorrect. Family composition does affect risk appetite.
Incorrect. There is no such non-linear relationship in the workbook.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) from an index fund?
options: ETF units trade on the exchange throughout the day, while index fund units are bought or sold from the AMC at end-of-day NAV
Index fund units trade on the exchange, while ETFs are bought only from the AMC
ETFs never involve brokerage or bid-ask costs
Index funds always have lower management costs than ETFs
questions.explanation: ETFs are index funds traded on the exchange with minute-to-minute prices, plus brokerage, demat and bid-ask costs. Index funds are transacted with the AMC at end-of-day NAV, with management costs that may be nominally higher.
hints: Correct. Exchange trading during the day vs AMC at end-of-day NAV.
Incorrect. This reverses the two.
Incorrect. ETFs do incur brokerage, demat and bid-ask costs.
Incorrect. Index fund management costs may be nominally higher than an ETF's.

questions.q: A retirement portfolio is 40% equity expected to earn 12% p.a. and 60% debt expected to earn 6% p.a. What is the blended expected return?
hints: Incorrect. This is a simple average of 12% and 6%, ignoring the weights.
Incorrect. 7.8% would need debt at 5%.
Incorrect. This adds the two returns.
